name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and reaches 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache is the bottleneck. Measured on the page (Tiger Lake i5-1135G7): C 0.555 ns/elt for 10k to 1M bytes; CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 5.2-5.9x (derived from page data); native build 0.0526 (10k), 0.0507 (30k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 7-10.6x (derived from page data). Also: selection from a small table 0.04 ns per element versus 0.2 ns, and a 35% advantage on a compiler benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs and the compiler line are on the page so it is reproducible. The C baseline is a simple scalar loop the author took from a Dyalog talk, not hand-vectorized C (a SIMD C version would win; the page says so), the benchmark density of 1/100 is described as not particularly favorable, and the speedup is a best case for BQN primitives. The algorithm is not the same in the strict sense: BQN uses a data-parallel mask and Replicate, C a sequential scan. Page is dated 2023 (gcc 12.2.1, clang 15.0.7) and CBQN has changed since.
found_via: github.com/mlochbaum/BQN docs/implementation listing, page 'Performance in BQN versus C' (versusc.html); CBQN README for licensing; no WebSearch used

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: Matmul time (median over runs, Xeon E-2324G): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, about 2.0x and 1.8x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s, Nim/gcc 3.091 s equal C. BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, Julia with OpenBLAS, Nim Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded here.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D: ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: This is a library-kernel difference, not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm is the same (transpose plus dot products) but the D reduction order differs, so results can differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1). The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'), unlike the BLAS rows which dominate the table. CPU model and flags are stated, but gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the D compilers' LLVM/GCC bases. Time includes allocation and matrix generation.
found_via: Direct read of kostya/benchmarks README Matmul table, matmul.c, matmul.d, common/commands.mk and dlang/phobos std/numeric.d (cross-language shared suite; no WebSearch query)

Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.

hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (elapsed time, hyperfine)

Mechanism is the searcher's inference, which would cap a claim at C if the verifier cannot confirm it; the reproducible harness and stated compilers and CPU class are why it is kept at B. name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (per search-result summary): up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA code that experts optimized over weeks or months, with 3-4x fewer lines. Results-table rows (labels matched by inference from a garbled extraction): local Laplacian 262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP vs about 62 algorithm + 7 schedule lines, 2.1x faster (secondary summary: 335 ms vs 158 ms); bilateral grid 5.9x faster, 3x shorter.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come from the WebSearch result summary of the PLDI 2013 paper (https://people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, host not reachable from this environment, so the PDF was not opened); the summarizer itself said the table text was garbled and matched rows by inference, and the abstract's 'up to 5x' disagrees with the 5.9x table row. Baselines are the paper authors' chosen 2012-13 hand-tuned implementations (not -O3 compiled naive code) on 2012 hardware; compiler flags and CPU models not confirmed. The repository does not carry the baselines or the paper's harness, so the claim is not reproducible from the repo alone (tier B, not A). The 'language' here is a C++-embedded DSL, so Halide pipelines are callable directly from C++.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Halide vs hand-tuned C++ speedup local Laplacian bilateral grid PLDI 2013 faster lines of code' (hits: people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, commit.csail.mit.edu copy, i-programmer.info summary); repo metadata from https://github.com/halide/Halide and raw LICENSE.txt

name: Bessels.jl
baseline: SpecialFunctions.jl wrappers: openlibm (C, FreeBSD msun) j0/y0/j1/y1/jn/yn for integer-order and order-0 and 1 calls, AMOS zbes* routines (Fortran, via openspecfun) for non-integer order, so only the order-0 and order-1 rows have a C baseline
workload: Float64 evaluation of Bessel J, Y, I, K functions and gamma for random x and order nu between 0 and 100.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (relative speed increase over SpecialFunctions.jl): besselj0 2.5x, bessely0 2.3x (the two rows whose baseline is openlibm C), besselj(nu,x) 6x, bessely(nu,x) 5x, besseli0 10x, besseli(nu,x) 7x, besselk0 10x, besselk(nu,x) 4x, Bessels.gamma 5x. README prose: 'in general 5-10x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.2 (no C/Fortran flags: baselines are prebuilt binary libraries)
hardware: Apple M1 run under Rosetta (x86 emulation)
why_faster: Different algorithms: piecewise polynomial/rational approximations per domain written in pure Julia that inline and vectorize, versus AMOS general-order series/recurrences and libm's older rational approximations.
tradeoffs: README admits accuracy is sometimes 'within a digit or two' of the baselines rather than better (its own error table vs ArbNumerics gives mean/max relative errors such as besselj0 3e-16/6e-14 and besselj(5.0,x) 3e-14/2e-11); positive real arguments mainly, limited complex support; Float64 focus.
caveats: First-party, run under Rosetta emulation, no compiler flags or CPU model beyond 'Apple M1', and speedups are ratios with no absolute times. Most of the baseline is Fortran AMOS, and a Fortran-vs-Julia comparison is outside this catalogue's scope; only besselj0/bessely0 (2.5x, 2.3x) are measured against C code, and the baseline goes through Julia ccall wrappers. Algorithm differs, so this is a library win, not a language win. The Bessels.gamma row is a re-export of Gamma.jl per the README, not Bessels' own code.

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (SciML)

tradeoffs: Best for short patterns (about 20 to 1000) over ASCII, DNA or IUPAC alphabets; needs AVX2 or NEON for full speed; Rust crate with C, Python, R and DuckDB bindings.
caveats: B rests on the README's citation of the peer-reviewed Bioinformatics paper (not opened); the numbers above are my ratios from the repo's CSV and the CPU is not stated on any page opened. Only the DNA profile without reverse complement was checked (other CSVs exist for other k values). Both tools do different work per match position (Sassy's text-direction tiling), so this is not the same algorithm.
found_via: Search 'Rust SIMD library beats C++ implementation peer-reviewed' led to Ragnar Groot Koerkamp's Rust tools; evals/README.md describes the Sassy vs Edlib eval
why_faster: README: bitpacking and SIMD (AVX2 and NEON) with the main novelty of tiling in the text direction.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (tsv-filter, tsv-select, tsv-summarize, tsv-join, csv2tsv)
baseline: GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU cut 8.25/8.29 and GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: April 2018 study: seven file-processing tasks on 1.7 to 4.8 GB TSV/CSV files (numeric row filter, regex row filter, column selection, narrow column selection, join, summary statistics, CSV to TSV), 10th percentile of 35 Linux runs.
claimed_speedup: Linux April 2018 (derived ratios from page data): numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 s vs mawk 11.31 s (2.1x) and GNU awk 42.80 s; column selection tsv-select 4.79 s vs mawk 9.51 s and GNU cut 14.46 s (3.0x); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 s vs GNU Datamash 48.51 s (3.1x). Losses: narrow column selection GNU cut 5.60 s beat tsv-select 8.26 s, and xsv (Rust) beat tsv-filter on the regex row filter (7.97 s vs 8.80 s) while mawk took 17.74 s.
compiler_and_flags: eBay tools: prebuilt release v1.1.19, built with LDC using LTO and PGO (per the study); C tools from OS package managers, flags unstated. The README recommends LDC with LTO and PGO for the fastest build.
hardware: Linux: commodity cloud VM with 16 Intel (Haswell) 2095 MHz CPUs, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04; macOS: Mac mini with a 3 GHz Intel i7 (2 cores), 16 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; DConf 2018 talk and D blog post
tradeoffs: Single-purpose tab-delimited tools without multithreading; CSV support only via csv2tsv; the study notes the comparison tools are not equivalent in features.
caveats: First-party study from 2018 (2017 and 2018 versions) with old tool versions. LTO and PGO are applied to the D side only, so optimisation levels are not matched, and the C tools are distro builds. The study itself notes comparisons between individual tools are less meaningful than the overall picture, and the narrow-column test and the regex filter were lost to GNU cut and xsv. Last commit 2021.
found_via: Noticed in the hck README benchmark table; then read docs/Performance.md and docs/comparative-benchmarks-2018.md in the repo
why_faster: Study attributes results to D written in a straightforward style, buffered output, and LTO/PGO builds (Linux gains of 7 to 46 percent between the 2017 and 2018 versions from LTO/PGO, output buffering and compiler improvements), plus single-purpose tools versus general Awk expression handling.

name: fd
baseline: GNU find (findutils, C), 'find -iregex' and 'find -iname'
workload: Search a home folder (about 750,000 subdirectories and 4 million files) for files ending in [0-9].jpg with a warm disk cache, timed with hyperfine; both tools returned the same 546 files.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms +- 10.0 vs find -iregex 19.922 s +- 0.109 (README: about 23x) and find -iname 11.226 s +- 0.104 (about 13x).
tradeoffs: Does not support all of find's options; respects .gitignore and hidden-file rules by default (the benchmark uses -u to disable them).
caveats: One query on one unnamed machine (README says so); find is single-threaded while fd walks directories in parallel, so this is a parallelism win and not a codegen win. GNU find version, locale and disk are not stated. The README links the sharkdp/fd-benchmarks repo for more tests, which was not opened.
found_via: Checked READMEs of widely used Rust command-line replacements for C tools
why_faster: README: parallelized directory traversal, with credit to the regex and ignore crates also used in ripgrep.

name: hck
baseline: GNU cut 8.30 (C) and mawk 1.3.4 (C)
workload: Select columns 1, 8 and 19 from a 7-million-line CSV (UCI all_train.csv), comma delimiter and a three-space delimiter, output to /dev/null, timed with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: Comma delimiter: hck -Ld, 1.198 s vs GNU cut 7.541 s +- 1.250 (README relative factor 6.30) and mawk 4.993 s (4.17). Three-space delimiter: hck -Ld'   ' 1.718 s vs 'tr -s | cut' 7.471 s (4.35). When hck is fed through the same tr pipeline it takes 6.171 s, equal to xsv and tsv-select; regex delimiters run 5 to 6x slower than hck's literal path.
compiler_and_flags: Rust and D tools compiled locally with optimizations (release binaries use PGO per README); GNU cut and mawk from the OS package manager, flags unstated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16 cores), 64 GB DDR4, 1 TB NVMe, Ubuntu 20
tradeoffs: Close to a drop-in for cut with a regex delimiter option; mmap path is on by default for files.
caveats: The README says the benchmarks are only meant to show hck is 'in the same ballpark' and are 'not authoritative'. PGO binaries against distro-built C tools, so optimisation levels are not matched. Single machine, 2020 era OS and tool versions.
found_via: Checked READMEs of Rust command-line replacements for C tools; hck benchmark also lists eBay tsv-utils

name: regex (Rust regex crate) as measured in the rebar barometer
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT), RE2 and Hyperscan
metric: throughput (search time); compile time is also reported
workload: rebar curated benchmark groups (literal, literal-alternate, date, ruff-noqa, lexer-veryl, cloud-flare-redos, unicode-character-data, words, aws-keys, bounded-repeat, unstructured-to-json, dictionary, noseyparker, quadratic) over haystacks such as OpenSubtitles text.
claimed_speedup: Search-time geometric mean of speed ratios to the best engine per benchmark (lower is better; 2025-12-19 record): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Engines ran different benchmark subsets, so these means are not a common-subset comparison. Single rows: sherlock-en 29.4 GB/s rust/regex vs 26.3 pcre2/jit, 12.1 re2, 32.0 hyperscan; sherlock-ru 35.6 GB/s vs 32.8, 768.1 MB/s, 4.3 GB/s; but sherlock-casei-en 10.5 GB/s vs 18.8 pcre2/jit and 29.2 hyperscan.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. Rust engines are release builds by rebar's harness; PCRE2, RE2 and Hyperscan are built by rebar's engine scripts with flags not shown on the pages opened.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K (from record/curated/2025-12-19/lscpu.txt in the rebar repo)
tradeoffs: Linear-time guarantees (no backreferences or lookaround), so it is not a drop-in for PCRE2 features. Compile time is much worse than PCRE2 in rebar (compile-time geometric mean 11.85 vs 1.41 for plain PCRE2 and 6.20 for PCRE2 JIT).
caveats: The suite is written and run by the regex crate's author, and the README calls its results a 'curated and biased' set whose analysis is mostly about the Rust crate. Hyperscan has a better search-time mean (2.37) and wins several rows, and PCRE2 JIT wins the case-insensitive literal rows. The record is close to tier A (public harness, lscpu.txt recorded) but build flags of the C engines were not confirmed, so it is left at C for the verifier to retier. Means cover different benchmark counts per engine.
found_via: Looked up the rebar README results after the memchr README pointed at it; rust-lang/regex page says benchmarks moved to rebar
why_faster: The rebar README attributes wins to literal optimizations and prefilters: memchr and the Teddy SIMD multi-substring algorithm (ported out of Hyperscan), lazy DFA, one-pass DFA and a Pike VM fallback selected by a meta engine.

name: sd
baseline: GNU sed (C), with and without -E
workload: Replace a quote character across about 1.5 GB of JSON; regex replacement '(\w+)' -> '$1$1' on a 55 MB JSON file; literal and regex replacement on a 1M-line, 36 MB file in sd's across and line-by-line modes; timed with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: Simple replacement: sd 0.997 s vs sed 2.338 s (-E) and 2.365 s (about 2.35x). Regex replacement on 55 MB: sd 0.942 s vs sed 11.315 s and 11.239 s (about 11.9x). On 1M lines: sd -A (across) 125.6 ms vs sed 316.4 ms for the literal; the default line-by-line mode takes 357.0 ms, slower than sed, for the literal; for the regex sd takes 566.7 ms (line-by-line) or 254.0 ms (across) vs sed 4432.7 ms.
tradeoffs: Different regex syntax from sed (Rust regex crate) and a different command interface; the across mode reads whole input, trading memory for speed (the README reports a peak RSS table).
caveats: First-party hyperfine run; no machine, sed version or locale is stated, and GNU sed regex speed varies a lot with locale. The README itself shows sd's default mode is slower than sed for plain literal replacement.
found_via: Checked READMEs of Rust command-line replacements for C tools
why_faster: README gives no mechanism beyond using Rust's regex crate and an across-file mode.

name: skani
baseline: FastANI (C++) and Mash (C++) for genome average nucleotide identity
workload: Average nucleotide identity computation between prokaryotic genomes and against a database of more than 65,000 genomes.
claimed_speedup: README: indexing/sketching about 3x faster than Mash, and querying about 25x faster than FastANI (but slower than Mash). No timings, datasets or hardware appear on the page.
tradeoffs: Approximate ANI without base-level alignment; accuracy is 'almost as accurate' as BLAST-based methods per README.
caveats: The peer-reviewed Nature Methods paper named in the README was not opened, so this stays at C although it may deserve B. The 25x figure is README prose without raw numbers, and the algorithm differs from FastANI's, so it is not a language effect.
found_via: Rust bioinformatics tools with C++ incumbents; skani README
why_faster: README: approximate mapping with sparse chaining of seed matches instead of base-level alignment.

name: Usuba (bitslicing language and compiler to C with SIMD intrinsics)
baseline: Hand-tuned bitsliced C reference implementations (the repo logs a DES comparison named 'bsc')
metric: throughput (units not stated in the log, probably cycles per byte)
workload: Bitsliced DES generated by Usuba vs the hand-tuned reference DES in experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc.
claimed_speedup: results.org logs des-usuba 17.086 +- 0.121 vs des-bsc 17.419 +- 0.142, about 1.9 percent lower (derived from page data; units unstated). The PLDI 2019 abstract (seen only in a search snippet, not opened) says the generated code is on par with hand-tuned references; the earlier WPMVP 2018 paper is quoted as 15 percent faster on DES depending on the C compiler.
tradeoffs: Domain-specific language for bitsliced and vector-sliced ciphers; targets x86 SIMD and the generated code is only as good as the C compiler used.
caveats: The win is within noise and the papers were not opened. results.org also records failed runs ('No supercop', 'C compilation goes wrong', a stack overflow). Kept as a language-level data point for the verifier; the claim is 'on par', not clearly 'faster'.
found_via: WebSearch 'Usuba bitslicing compiler faster than hand-written C ciphers PLDI github usubalang'
why_faster: Compiler-level optimizations specific to bitslicing (inlining, scheduling, interleaving; the repo has bench directories for each).

name: Vibrato
baseline: MeCab (C++ morphological analyzer) with IPADIC 2.7.0 and UniDic 3.1.1
workload: Tokenize 2,346 sentences (about 158.8 characters each) of 'I Am a Cat' (Aozora Bunko), elapsed time averaged over 100 runs.
claimed_speedup: 42 ms vs 87 ms with IPADIC (about 2.1x, derived from page data) and 75 ms vs 179 ms with UniDic (about 2.4x, derived from page data). The raw-connector UniDic model takes 1364 ms and the dual-connector model 170 ms, about MeCab's UniDic time.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (the wiki lists Vibrato 0.5.0 and MeCab 2020-09-14 but no build flags)
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K (16 cores), 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Reimplementation of MeCab's minimum-cost method; models must be compiled into Vibrato's format. The UniDic model is 717 MB in the standard form, and the smaller variants trade speed (252 MB raw-connector at 1364 ms, 300 MB dual-connector at 170 ms).
caveats: First-party benchmark (README figure plus wiki), MeCab build flags unknown, single corpus and machine. The two NLP2023 conference papers listed in the README are about cache efficiency and CRF score splitting; their numbers were not opened.
found_via: Checked READMEs of Rust library crates with C/C++ originals; README points to the Speed-Comparison wiki
why_faster: README: cache-efficient id mappings for the large connection matrix, plus a simplified implementation of the MeCab algorithm.
